Opening statement

Dad, here’s what Saturday means.

“D and I have been playing a long, story-driven game together for about a month. We started while he was out of work, and since he got his full-time job, it’s been harder to find time to finish.

We’re setting aside Saturday for the final chapter. It may take the whole day, so please count me out of Uncle’s piano performance from 5 to 7. I know seeing your brother play matters to you. This is meaningful time with my brother, too.

I want us to experience the ending together, without watching the clock. And afterward, I’d love to show you why this particular game has us so invested—starting with the music.”

— J, with D very much part of the story

That is the entire request. The exhibits below explain the joy behind it.

Exhibit A / The facts

A calendar problem.
A brotherhood solution.

Adult life makes shared time surprisingly difficult to arrange. D getting a job is good news. It also changed the rhythm of something his brother and he had started together.

2brothers in one shared playthrough
1month since this adventure began
~100hours: the scale of the story, not an audited save-file reading
1Saturday set aside to try to reach the ending
01 / THE OPENING SET

We began together.

J and D started the playthrough while D was unemployed. The adventure became something they were sharing across a stretch of ordinary life.

02 / THE TEMPO CHANGED

Work entered the arrangement.

D got a full-time job. The game was postponed. The enthusiasm remained; the convenient opportunities to act on it became fewer.

03 / SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 14

We made room for the finale.

Both brothers have busy lives. They are deliberately reserving a day, with enough room for the ending to take the time it takes.

The scarce resource is two brothers’ shared availability.

Stipulated for the record: J had not previously committed to attending the performance. This is advance notice of a scheduling choice. No allegation is made against the piano, the pianist, or the fine institution of live jazz.

Exhibit B / Translating the medium

Begin with Rayman.
Then change the verbs.

Imagine a long ensemble drama in which you also manage the characters’ days, build their relationships, and conduct their battles.

Persona 5 Royal is an expanded version of Atlus’s Persona 5. You play a student in Tokyo who leads the Phantom Thieves: an unlikely circle of friends confronting people who abuse their power. Ordinary school days alternate with fantastical heists inside distorted mental worlds. [1]

The astonishing move is to give both halves weight. A conversation in a café and a spectacular supernatural battle belong to the same life. The small moments make you care what happens in the large ones.

Rayman 2 is a wonderful reference point: exploration, imaginative worlds, obstacles, music, and the satisfaction of learning how to get somewhere. Persona places much more of its attention on reading a situation, choosing a response, developing people, and planning ahead.

Knowing Rayman is a doorway into games. The next step is discovering how widely different games can ask us to participate—much as a film musical and a courtroom drama use the same screen for very different pleasures.

A change of emphasis, with affection for both games
The questionRayman 2: The Great EscapePersona 5 Royal
What am I practicing?Movement, timing, exploration, navigating a fantastic world.Judgment, preparation, recognizing patterns, combining abilities.
What moves me forward?Overcoming physical obstacles and discovering the route.Story events, relationships, calendar decisions, and tactical battles.
What does success feel like?“I can finally make that jump.”“We understand this system—and we care what happens to these people.”

These are broad emphases, not exclusive categories: Rayman has story and puzzles; Persona also has exploration and movement.

JRPG

A Japanese role-playing game. Here, that means an authored adventure built around characters, developing abilities, exploration, and strategic encounters. It is a genre label, not a test you need to study for.

Persona

A supernatural expression of a character’s inner self, used in battle. Joker can work with many of them. Think mythological stagecraft meeting a customizable repertoire.

Palace

A place where someone’s distorted view of the world becomes architecture. You explore an argument made into rooms: a psychological metaphor you can walk through.

“Metaverse” here names the game’s cognitive otherworld. No headset, cryptocurrency, or meeting with a virtual real-estate agent is involved.

Exhibit C / For the IT mind

A beautifully
interconnected system.

A good system becomes interesting when one decision changes what other decisions are possible. Persona turns that principle into a daily life.

You shape the person who faces the next challenge.

Spend time with someone, learn what matters to them, and become more capable together. Use a quiet evening to prepare. Spend tomorrow’s limited energy wisely. The adventure remembers enough of those choices for your routine to feel like it belongs to you.

The feedback loop / schematic, not a literal formula

Friendship is part of the architecture.

Time & attentionChoose how to spend a day
→
RelationshipsGet to know a Confidant
→
New supportUnlock useful abilities
→
More possibilitiesPrepare and explore effectively

Confidants are characters whose developing bonds can grant practical benefits. The game makes attention to other people mechanically consequential. That is an unusually elegant way to connect its rules to its themes. [2]

Think dependencies, resources, and design.

An IT person can appreciate the pleasure of understanding how parts interact: limited time, money, health, skill energy, available teammates, and enemy vulnerabilities. A seemingly minor improvement can make the whole operation more resilient.

Joker’s Personas are a repertoire you can configure. Fusion lets you combine Personas into others and select eligible inherited skills. The interesting question becomes: What capabilities does this group need, and what weaknesses have we left exposed? [3]

The analogy has a limit. These are written characters with emotional lives, and the pleasure of knowing them exceeds the utility they provide. A friend is more than an upgrade path, even when the interface offers one.

A well-designed game lets understanding become a kind of power.

Try it / a tiny day in Tokyo

You have choices. You don’t have every choice.

Pick one afternoon and one evening activity. Watch how the emphasis of your day changes.

After school
Evening

People + preparation. An afternoon strengthens a bond; an evening prepares a resource for a future outing.

You cannot spend that same afternoon studying. Choosing creates the shape of your day.

Simplified illustration, not a game planner. In Royal, activities depend on dates, access, weather, story events, and other restrictions. The combinations here demonstrate tradeoffs, not a guaranteed in-game schedule.

Try it / conduct a miniature battle

Spot the opening. Pass the spotlight.

In this simplified encounter, three enemies have three different weaknesses. Take as long as you like.

♜Enemy AWeak to FIRE
♞Enemy BWeak to ELEC.
♝Enemy CWeak to WIND
ANN / fireRYUJI / elec.MORGANA / wind
Read the room.Ann can exploit Enemy A’s fire weakness. A weakness hit that knocks a standing enemy down earns an extra action: “1 More.”

Full sequence: fire → extra action → Baton Pass → electricity → Baton Pass → wind → all enemies down → All-Out Attack.

Original schematic, not game footage. Damage values, resistances, resource costs, and many other rules are omitted. One human player commands the fictional party. [3]

For the guitarist, another translation

The rules are the changes.
Your decisions are the performance.

In a jazz group, knowing the tune creates room for choices: when to leave space, when to support someone else, when to take a phrase somewhere new. In Persona’s battles, knowing the rules lets you recognize an opening and give the right person the next move.

The Baton Pass makes that handoff literal. A successful setup can become another teammate’s stronger opportunity. The delight comes from the sequence clicking: one person creates space for another. It is a satisfying image of competence shared across an ensemble.

You have time to think while selecting battle commands. The spectacle can look frantic; the underlying decision can be considered. You can ask, “Who should go next?” without having to make the decision at the speed of a guitar solo.

The button press is the visible tip of the thought.

This is a metaphor for coordination. Persona’s combat does not require you to play in musical time; its jazz soundtrack is not a rhythm-game input test.

Exhibit D / Call the music to the stand

Dad, you already
speak this language.

Listen for groove, space, harmonic color, and a singer who knows how to sit inside an arrangement. There is a direct route into this world through your ears.

Composer Shoji Meguro describes Persona 5’s musical foundation in terms of acid jazz. Royal’s music team, including Toshiki Konishi, extends that palette. Lyn gives its vocal tracks their distinctive presence. In the composers’ interview, Meguro describes making “No More What Ifs” sound like a singer performing inside a jazz club. [4]

So here is a listening invitation, from one musical world to another. Hear how the bass gives a phrase direction, how accompaniment can be sparse and still feel complete, and how a groove can make a place feel inhabited. The game’s atmosphere grows through repetition: a piece returns, and eventually it feels like arriving somewhere you know.

01

“Beneath the Mask”

Listen for: how much personality can live in restraint. Notice the relationship between the vocal phrase and the accompaniment. Ask what makes a recording feel like somewhere you could stay.

02

“No More What Ifs”

Listen for: the intimacy of the vocal and the room left around it. Royal actually contains a jazz club. The connection to your musical life is unusually literal. [4]

03

“Take Over”

Listen for: what happens when the arrangement steps into a brighter, more assertive register. Meguro specifically describes adding brass and strings for Royal’s ambush-battle music. [4]

An audible analogy / four bars, four roles

Build a little ensemble.

Start the sketch, then bring voices in and out. Hear how a steady bass, harmonic color, rhythmic punctuation, and a pulse occupy different spaces.

Dm9ii · OPEN
G13V · LEAN FORWARD
Cmaj9I · ARRIVE
A7VI · TURN AROUND
40%96 BPM · lightly swung eighths

Silent until you press Play. No network connection needed.

An original synthesized teaching sketch, not a Persona track, transcription, or recreation. Its familiar ii–V–I–VI turnaround illustrates ensemble roles; it makes no claim about the game’s actual chord progressions. The real recordings are far richer than these simple browser voices.

Exhibit E / The scale of the undertaking

A hundred hours
is room to belong.

The number matters because it suggests how much familiarity can accumulate: routines, places, personalities, music, small victories, and the memory of learning how it all fits together.

Each square = 1 hour. Colors are decorative, not categories.

50two-hour films’ worth of time100 hours ÷ 2 hours per film
133.345-minute albums’ worth of time100 hours ÷ 0.75 hours per album

A comparison of duration only. This does not make one game artistically equivalent to fifty films, and it is not a forecast of tomorrow’s remaining playtime. Actual playthrough lengths vary. The hundred-hour scale comes from the way J described this adventure.

The achievement of learning

You begin by asking what each option means. Later, you can see a combination, prepare for a problem, and make an informed decision. The game turns a confusing interface into a language you can speak.

The achievement of staying

A long work asks for sustained attention. You hold its cast, rules, and themes in your head long enough for a small return or a changed relationship to mean something. You earn the perspective from which the finale lands.

The achievement of sharing

You carry a complicated experience with another person through changing circumstances. Finishing gives the two of you a completed chapter in your own history: “Remember when we played that together?”

Time spent gives the ending a history.
Sharing it gives the history a witness.

There is no need to inflate this into a professional qualification. It is a meaningful leisure achievement: commitment, growing competence, emotional investment, and a shared undertaking carried to its conclusion. A musician already knows that an accomplishment can matter deeply without appearing on a résumé.

Exhibit F / Why the final act deserves room

The third semester:
the theme returns changed.

“Third semester” refers to the school calendar inside the story. Royal adds a major late-game story arc. It is the particular stretch J and D are seeking to finish. [2]

01

Establish the world.

Meet people, learn its language, find a rhythm. Characters gradually become familiar enough for their decisions to carry weight.

The tune enters your ear.

02

Hear it differently.

Royal’s added final arc tests and extends the themes developed across the earlier journey. Familiar ideas are placed under new pressure.

The harmony changes beneath it.

03

Let it resolve.

The conclusion gives the accumulated experience a shape. There is pleasure in seeing what a work finally asks you to take away.

You hear the whole form.

A thematic diagram, not equal divisions of runtime or a map of the game’s literal chapters. No plot outcome is revealed here.

A finale can reorganize a whole work.

You know how the return of a melody can carry everything that happened while it was away. The notes are recognizable; the meaning has changed. Long-form storytelling has its own version of that experience. An early conversation can acquire weight you could not have heard at the beginning.

The developers describe Royal as deepening the existing game and building new themes on top of its earlier story. The added arc is designed to have a relationship with what came before. [5]

Experiencing it takes more than advancing text.

There are scenes to follow, decisions to consider, exploration and battles to play, and an ending to sit with. In a shared playthrough, there is also the other person: the glance, the reaction, the conversation that begins when something unexpected happens.

A relaxed block of time lets the brothers follow that sequence at its own pace. They cannot promise the exact moment they will finish. They can decide to give the attempt a proper place in their day.

FIN.

We want to reach the end with enough attention left to feel it—and with the person who was there at the beginning.

Finishing the story is the goal described here. That does not imply every trophy, every optional challenge, or 100% completion. Detailed discussion of Royal’s moral questions is reserved for the spoiler appendix.

Exhibit G / The heart of the case

Two sets.
Two kinds of brotherhood.

Dad, the reason you want to hear your brother play is already the beginning of the explanation. The music matters. So does the fact that it is your brother making it.

Our experience has that second layer, too. Persona is the work we are finishing; the playthrough is something J and D have made together by being there for it. Both things deserve to be named.

Persona 5 Royal is a single-player game. Our shared playthrough is a social way of experiencing it. Two people can care about a decision, follow the same story, and celebrate an outcome even when the software accepts one controller. [1]

A record does not become a two-player record when two people listen closely together. The listening still becomes something they share. The same is true here.

The ending belongs to the game.
The memory will belong to us.

This parallel does not erase the disappointment of missing the set. Two worthwhile plans can overlap. Respecting one another means being able to explain a choice, hear that it matters, and accept that no family can attend every meaningful thing at once.

Cross-examination / Fair questions, straight answers

The court recognizes
a raised eyebrow.

The defense will now answer the reasonable objections. Counsel has been instructed to stop referring to a Saturday as a “once-in-a-civilization event.”

“Can’t you just pause it?”

Yes, we can stop playing and resume later from a save. The important constraint is finding another good block of time when both of us are free. We want an uninterrupted finale because that is how we would most enjoy sharing it.

The honest request is to respect a chosen plan. We are not claiming that the console will explode if we leave the room.

“Why does that take the whole day?”

It might, rather than definitely will. Our remaining progress, reading pace, battles, breaks, and conversation determine the length. Reserving a day gives us room to try without promising an exact finish time we do not know.

That is why J is saying in advance that he will not attend the 5–7 PM performance. A clear answer now is more considerate than an optimistic “maybe” followed by a last-minute cancellation.

“But this is your uncle playing live.”

That matters. A live set is a particular occasion, and wanting your family there is understandable. J had not committed to attending this one, and he is choosing the time he and D have reserved together.

He can wish his uncle a great set and ask about another opportunity to hear him. A recording, if one happens to exist, would be a nice bonus; nobody is being assigned the job of producing one, and it would not reproduce being there.

“Are a hundred hours automatically an achievement?”

A stopwatch alone proves duration. The meaningful part is what those hours contain: learning a complicated game, following a substantial story, developing a shared reference point, and making time to bring it to a close.

Past time spent also creates no obligation to keep going. J and D want to finish because the experience still matters to them. Their enthusiasm, rather than a debt to the save file, is the reason for Saturday.

“Wouldn’t watching the ending online do the same thing?”

It could tell us what happens. Playing brings the characters and abilities we have developed into the conclusion and asks us to act. The anticipation of doing it, the moment a plan works, and our own pace through the scenes are part of what we have been sharing.

You can read a review of a concert and learn the set list. You still understand why someone might want the experience itself.

“Do you want me to think this is more important than music?”

No. We want you to understand why this particular story and this particular time together are important to us. You do not have to rank the arts, adopt our tastes, or play a hundred hours to take that seriously.

And given your interest in jazz and systems, we suspect there is more here for you to enjoy than the phrase “beating a video game” suggests.

“Would I actually enjoy it?”

Possibly—and the best evidence would be a small, relaxed introduction. Your ear for music and interest in systems give you useful ways in. Your taste will decide the rest.

It is dialogue-heavy, stylized, and often about young people. It also deals with abuse of authority, shame, belonging, responsibility, and the difficulty of acting well. Its wit, absurdity, earnestness, and darker material coexist. You can enjoy some of that, dislike some of it, and have an entirely fair response.

Closing argument / Submitted with love

Let the record show:
this is time together.

The motion, stripped of all theatrical legal stationery

“Dad, we’re spending Saturday finishing something we started together. D’s new job has made that time harder to find, and we’re glad we’ve made room for it. Please count me out of the 5–7 PM performance. I hope your brother has a great set. This is a special day with mine.”

J + D · Saturday, November 14, 2026

The finding we hope for

“I understand why you care about this. Enjoy finishing it together. Tell me about it afterward.”

The perfectly acceptable encore

“And play me that jazz-club song. I’d like to hear what all the fuss is about.”

A standing invitation / No hundred-hour commitment required

Dad, take the guest chair.

You do not need to become a gamer before you are allowed to be curious. Let us give you a twenty-minute tour another time.

01

Listen first.

Choose a track and give it your musician’s attention. Tell us what you hear in the harmony, phrasing, rhythm, and arrangement. We would like to hear it through your ears.

About 5 minutes.

02

Visit the ordinary world.

Let us show you a spoiler-safe café or city scene. Look at how music, design, dialogue, and tiny routines make a fictional place feel familiar.

About 5 minutes.

03

Call a few plays.

Try a simple battle with us explaining the menu. Decide who should act and why. We can handle unfamiliar controls while you get a feel for the decisions.

About 10 minutes.

If you want to go further, begin a fresh game of Persona 5 Royal with us nearby. We can explain the interface, help you find a comfortable difficulty, and let the opening introduce its people at its own pace. There is plenty of reading, so a twenty-minute tour is a sample of the experience, not the full opening act.

You can also just listen to the soundtrack, watch a little, or ask us what we liked. Curiosity is enough. The invitation is to discover a work we care about—and perhaps to make the next shared memory a three-person one.

For the already initiated / Entirely optional

SEALED EXHIBIT · MAJOR THIRD-SEMESTER AND ENDING SPOILERSOpen the deeper argument: what Royal’s final act is really asking.

Opening this exhibit reveals the central antagonist, an identity revelation, the final moral choice, and aspects of the ending. J and D can save it until after they finish. Dad can skip it and still understand the entire request.

The most disturbing administrator is the one who means well.

Takuto Maruki can reshape reality to relieve suffering. The offer is emotionally serious: losses repaired, frustrated wishes fulfilled, painful lives made easier. Royal gives benevolent control a sympathetic face, then asks what that benevolence licenses its author to do. [S1]

Here is the IT analogy at its most useful. Imagine someone with unrestricted administrative access who can change not only the system’s behavior, but the users’ memories and preferences. A satisfied user base would no longer be enough to prove that the system respects its users. The mechanism that measures approval would itself be under the administrator’s control.

If a perfect system makes dissent disappear, its dashboard cannot tell you whether anyone is free.

That is an interpretation of the story’s ethical design, not a literal cybersecurity model. It helps explain why the final conflict has more bite than “defeat the person who wants bad things.” The offer contains things these characters have every reason to want. Refusing it costs something, which makes the response reveal a value.

Sumire: relief and identity

The revelation that the girl known as Kasumi is her grieving sister Sumire makes the question intimate. Maruki’s intervention offers relief through an altered sense of who she is. [S2]

The philosophical issue is whether another person can resolve your pain by deciding which version of you gets to exist. A humane reading should keep two thoughts together: help can be necessary and good; the person receiving it still matters as an author of her own life. Suffering is not made virtuous merely by being real.

Akechi: agency at a possible cost

Akechi refuses to let Maruki determine his life, even when rejecting that world is presented as threatening his continued existence. The emotional force comes from his insistence on owning the decision. [S1]

His ultimate fate remains deliberately ambiguous; the creators leave room for interpretation. Treating one explanation as settled canon flattens what the game withholds. His stance is clearest precisely where the outcome is uncertain. [S3]

A theme can return in a more difficult key.

The earlier adventure repeatedly stages resistance to exploitative authority. Royal complicates that grammar by asking what happens when authority offers comfort and believes it is helping. “Choose for yourself” sounds uncomplicated until choosing means accepting loss, difficulty, and a future no one has guaranteed.

That is why the semester earns its place in a long work. The player has spent so much time with these people that their wishes arrive with emotional context. A summary can state the dilemma. Accumulated familiarity makes the offer tempting.

The music and the mechanics join the argument.

Even the late-game titles—“Keep Your Faith,” “Throw Away Your Mask,” and “Our Light”—invite a listener to hear conviction, persuasion, and farewell as different emotional positions. Listen after finishing, when the titles have room to resonate. The change in musical character can make the final stretch feel like a new interpretation of the world you already knew.

Meanwhile, the habit of building a team and passing opportunities between its members gives the player a practical experience of mutual dependence. The friendship theme has lived in conversations and in decisions. By the end, the idea of acting together has a history in your hands.

The ending’s quiet achievement is permission to move forward.

In Royal’s ending following the rejection of Maruki’s world, the friends face lives that will take them in different directions. [S1] One reading is that a bond can survive without keeping everyone permanently inside the same beautiful moment. Friendship can make leaving possible.

There is a gentle resonance with J and D’s circumstances. D’s new job is life moving forward. Setting aside a Saturday lets the brothers honor something they shared while making room for the lives they now have. They do not need to preserve the exact conditions under which the playthrough began in order to give it an ending.

That is the deeper case for the finale: finishing a story about time, choice, and connection can itself become a small act of choosing time for connection.

[S1] Plot reference: Persona 5 — Royal plot summary. Used for the basic events; the ethical and musical readings above are this essay’s interpretations.

[S2] Character reference: List of Persona 5 characters, for Sumire’s identity and Maruki’s intervention.

[S3] Developer commentary: P5R Official Complete Guide interview, English fan translation, especially the discussion of Akechi’s unresolved fate. Translation is unofficial; the destination may require sign-in.
